summary: Examines issues with how the IPv4 address space was being managed and what might result as the pool of unallocated addresses shrinks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The numbered mailboxes of the internet were running out, and this note asks what happens when they do.

questions: what happens when ipv4 addresses run out
how should internet addresses be allocated
subtitle: An early analysis of how IPv4 address allocation policies might shape the Internet when addresses run out.

tldr.problem: IPv4 addresses are a finite resource being allocated freely on a first-come, first-served basis, and projections suggested they would run out within 6 to 12 years.
tldr.mechanism: This memo examines what happens if current allocation policies continue unchanged, what happens if pricing or lease-based models are introduced, and the governance challenges either scenario raises.
tldr.outcome: It warns that unregulated free market trading in addresses after exhaustion could lead to monopolies and restrict fair access, but pricing policies face political and bureaucratic barriers.

today: RFC 1744 is informational. The predictions about exhaustion and market dynamics proved largely accurate; IPv4 addresses became scarce and expensive in secondary markets. The shift to regional registries and eventual adoption of IPv6 reflects the concerns raised here. Address market pricing and lease models were never adopted in the original IANA/ICANN process for historical and political reasons the RFC identifies.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Every device on the Internet needs a unique IPv4 address to send and receive data. The author, Geoff Huston, examines how these addresses have been allocated and managed since the protocol's design in the early 1980s.

IPv4 addresses are 32-bit numbers, providing a theoretical maximum of 2^32 (about 4.3 billion) unique addresses. In the mid-1990s, growth in Internet use made clear that this pool was finite. Current allocation practices—free, first-come, first-served, and once-and-for-all—were not tied to any cost or time limit. The author notes that projections from the IETF Address Lifetime Expectancy Working Group expected the unallocated pool to be exhausted in 6 to 12 years.
sections.eli5: When the Internet started, there were billions of numbered mailboxes available, and anyone who needed them could grab as many as they wanted, for free, with no limit. But so many new networks started using the Internet that the supply would run out.

sections.title: How Current Allocation Shapes Future Markets
sections.content:
The memo observes that the IPv4 address space has become a valuable economic resource: entities can conduct direct communication and commerce because addresses are unique and globally recognized. This creates market incentives.

Under current free allocation, once the unallocated pool is exhausted, a secondary market in addresses is inevitable. Entities that claimed large blocks early could resell unused portions to new entrants, creating profit opportunities. The RFC predicts that such trading would initially reduce inefficiency (underutilized blocks would be reallocated to users needing them), but would eventually concentrate in the hands of large Internet Service Providers, who have both the inventory and the market power to dominate trading. The author warns of risks including monopoly pricing, barriers to entry for smaller providers, and the ISPs controlling the registries that validate ownership—effectively becoming both merchants and title offices.
sections.eli5: If rules don't change, whoever grabbed the biggest pile of address numbers early could sell them later for lots of money. Big companies would end up controlling most of the supply and could charge whatever they wanted.

sections.title: Proposed: Pricing and Lease-Based Allocation
sections.content:
To encourage efficient use and extend the pool's lifetime, the RFC proposes moving from free, permanent allocation to a lease-based system with pricing. Under this model, allocations would be temporary (like a lease) and cost money, creating economic incentives for efficiency.

Higher prices for larger blocks would encourage equitable access across a diversity of entities. Pricing could be scaled to account for the cost of renumbering (the technical effort required to swap addresses in deployed networks) and to motivate adoption of alternatives like dynamic address assignment and Network Address Translation. The lessee would have a right of first renewal at lease end, maintaining a market value for held blocks.

This approach could be applied to all future allocations, or retroactively to existing blocks (with transition provisions to honor the implicit permanence of earlier free allocations). The memo notes that pricing alone is insufficient—it must be paired with policy design to be effective.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving out unlimited addresses for free, charge a rent for them—higher rent for bigger blocks. This would make companies use only what they actually need and force them to give back unused space.

sections.title: The Governance Problem
sections.content:
The memo's core tension is that pricing and lease models make economic sense but have proven politically infeasible in practice. Two barriers stand out.

First, there is uncertain ownership of the address space. The IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) has managed the pool via consensus-driven Internet standards processes, not formal property law. Declaring ownership and imposing pricing policies unilaterally has not gained community consensus. Second, the address space is neither recognized as a public resource (like radio spectrum or telephone numbers, managed by national authorities) nor as a private resource owned by a single entity. Recent policy changes have assigned large segments to international and regional bodies on a continuing free, first-come, first-served basis.

Without ability to implement pricing, the author outlines three possible outcomes: (a) management taken over by national governments, which risks heavy-handed regulation that stifles innovation; (b) management by ISPs, which creates conflicts of interest and risk of monopolistic behavior; or (c) inadequate funding and poor administration of the registration and allocation function.
sections.eli5: The tricky part is that nobody clearly owns the Internet's address numbers—they're managed by volunteers using consensus, not like property. So charging for them sounds logical but hits political walls, and each way forward has problems.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that absent a major policy shift, the Internet will continue free allocation until exhaustion, after which open-market trading will take over. The result may be monopoly-based pricing and restricted access—what the author calls policy failure.

However, the memo frames this as not entirely bad: the inability of free allocation to sustain IPv4 is precisely the economic pressure that is driving design and deployment of IPv6, with its vastly larger address space. A key message is that if IPv6 or a successor technology is to succeed, it must learn from this experience and show better address management discipline. The immediate recommendation is for the Internet community to examine management structures that include both pricing and policy, and apply them to both current IPv4 and any successor technology.
sections.eli5: The memo says: unless rules change, the free supply will end in problems. But maybe that's okay if it pushes people to use better technology with more addresses. The real lesson is to do it better next time.

references.text: Gerich, E., "Guidelines for Management of IP Address Space", RFC 1466, Merit Network, Inc., May 1993.
